newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler quits 6-year Cap Gemini stake.
newsitem.headline: Daimler quits 6-year Cap Gemini stake.

text.p: Industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG said on Wednesday it would quit its six-year stake in computer systems firm Cap Gemini SA, killing speculation it planned a take-over of the French company.
Daimler said in a statement it would pull out of Gap Gemini because of differing strategic focuses and because a U.S. Bank Holding Company Act hindered Cap Gemini's business there.
The German company said it would sell its 24.4 percent stake in Cap Gemini "in the medium term" using a convertible bond which would generate proceeds of more than one billion marks.
Chairman Juergen Schrempp said Daimler, Germany's largest company, will use the proceeds of the note sale to strengthen the Information Technology (IT) business of its services unit debis AG.
"In this way, this important business for the Daimler-Benz group will be able to support its own growth," Schrempp said.

A Daimler spokesman said debis had developed a different strategic focus than Cap Gemini, targeting capital intensive business and outsourcing where the French company was primarily engaged in software.
But the partnership also faced obstacles in the U.S.
Under the U.S.-Bank-Holding-Company-Act, Gap Gemini's businesses faced restrictions because Deutsche Bank AG holds a stake in Daimler.

Daimler maintains that stake is 24.4 percent, but U.S. authorities, using a different measure of ownership, concluded that Deutsche's real stake exceeded 25 percent -- a level that brought limitations on Cap Gemini's ability to do business, especially with U.S. banks.
Daimler's decision follows a report in the French newspaper La Tribune that Cap Gemini wanted the German group to give up its shareholding.

"Cap can manage on its own...It is better that debis leaves," the newspaper reported without giving a source. Daimler and Cap first signed an alliance in 1991 amid hopes of a larger industrial alliance.
Only in April, debis chairman Klaus Mangold was quoted as saying the Daimler unit might increase its stake in Cap to a majority holding.
"In Europe and the U.S. there is enormous demand at present for shares in information technology companies," a German newspaper reported Mangold as saying.
Mangold said in the statement on Wednesday that his company could may still cooperage with Cap Gemini on specific projects and that he expected Cap Gemini's share price to climb.
Daimler said proceeds from the exchangeable note offering will allow debis to "significantly expand" its international operations in the information systems management market.
Although Daimler still faces the same problems under U.S. bank-holding rules as Cap Gemini, the debis unit has a significantly less active business in North America.
The notes will have a maturity of four-and-half years and can be exchanged, at the option of investors, into Cap Gemini shares.
They would be offered to investors from June 26 through a book-building exercise and pricing details are expected no later than June 30.

Although Daimler's withdrawal from Cap Gemini recalled recent strategic moves by Daimler to quit relationships with other less profitable companies, analysts said Wednesday's announcement was driven by strategic reasons.

"Daimler wants to expand its information technology business even if it can't do it with Gemini," said Lather Lubinetski, analyst at Enskilda Corporate in London. "This should be positive for Daimler's earnings."
